passage: The school trip bus had a puncture, and the lunch stop shrank to twenty minutes. Rukmini, fifteen, opened her steel tiffin under a tree. A boy from the back row grinned. "Jains can't eat after dark, right? Is your family scared of ghosts?" A few laughed. Rukmini's face went hot and she closed the lid halfway. "It's not a joke," she said, but her voice came out small. Vandana, sitting beside her, said clearly, "That's her family's belief, and it's not funny. Would you laugh at your grandmother's fast?" The boy shrugged. Ms. Narang, the teacher, had overheard. When the bus started, she stood at the front. "Making fun of what a family believes is not humour. The ghost idea is simply wrong. Rukmini, I'm sorry that happened." Rukmini nodded and finally took a bite.

qa.q: What did the boy from the back row ask Rukmini?
qa.a: The boy asked whether Jains can't eat after dark and whether Rukmini's family is scared of ghosts.

qa.q: How does Rukmini feel when the boy jokes, and what shows it?
qa.a: Rukmini feels hurt and ashamed. Her face goes hot, she closes the lid halfway and her voice comes out small.

qa.q: Which choice by Ms. Narang helped protect Rukmini?
qa.a: Ms. Narang spoke to everyone on the bus, said that mocking a family's belief is not humour, named the ghost idea as wrong, and apologised to Rukmini.

qa.q: How might Vandana see the boy's joke?
qa.a: As unkind and unfair. She says it is her friend's family's belief and asks whether he would laugh at his own grandmother's fast.

grounding: A teenager hears a joke about her religion from a classmate and feels ashamed, and a friend and a teacher speak up and call the stereotype false.

passage: In the Bengaluru school corridor, Uday, fourteen, had mentioned his church youth group when a classmate called out, "Careful, Uday will convert you!" Two boys laughed, and someone added, "They only make friends to convert people." Uday stared at his shoes. He wanted to say something clever, but nothing came out, and hot shame crept up his neck. Dev, who sat beside him in maths, stepped in. "Uday lent me his notes. That's all he's done." The boys drifted away. That afternoon Rekha Ma'am, the English teacher, heard about it from Dev and stopped the class. "The idea that a whole group of people all act one way is false, and it hurts real classmates. Nobody here is being recruited by anyone. If you have a question about a belief, ask it politely." Uday looked up. Dev gave him a small nod.

qa.q: Who stepped in when the classmates laughed at Uday?
qa.a: Dev, who sat beside Uday in maths, stepped in and said that Uday had only lent him notes.

qa.q: What is Uday feeling as he stares at his shoes?
qa.a: Uday feels ashamed and silenced. He wants to answer, but nothing comes out.

qa.q: What turning point protected Uday in the afternoon?
qa.a: Dev told Rekha Ma'am, and she stopped the class and named the idea as false, so the whole class heard that nobody was being recruited.

qa.q: How does Dev seem to see Uday?
qa.a: As a classmate and individual who lent notes, not as a stereotype. Dev speaks for Uday first and then reports it to the teacher.

grounding: A teenager hears a rumour about his faith from classmates and feels ashamed, and a friend and a teacher speak up and name the stereotype as false.

passage:
Dear Jeevan,
You asked how the new school in Leicester is. Mostly okay, even as the only Indian boy in my year. But something happened I want to tell someone.
In RE class, a boy asked if I "worship cows," and made mooing noises. Half the class laughed. Another said Hindus "have a million gods, how do you even keep track?" I went hot all over. I wanted to shout and I wanted to disappear, both at once. I said nothing.
Then my friend Maya said, loudly, "That's not funny. Stop." And Mr. Carter paused the lesson. He said, "That's a stereotype, and it's wrong. Raghav, would you like to share anything? You don't have to." I shook my head. He said he'd talk to the boys after class, and he did.
I felt better, but still a bit sick.
Write back soon,
Raghav

qa.q: Where is Raghav's new school?
qa.a: Raghav's new school is in Leicester.

qa.q: How did Raghav feel when the class laughed?
qa.a: Raghav went hot all over, feeling angry and ashamed, wanting both to shout and to disappear.

qa.q: How did Maya and Mr. Carter protect Raghav?
qa.a: Maya spoke up loudly, and Mr. Carter paused the lesson, named it as a false stereotype, offered Raghav a choice to speak, and talked to the boys after class.

qa.q: What would change if nobody had spoken up?
qa.a: Raghav might keep feeling silenced and ashamed, and the boys might think such jokes were acceptable.

grounding: A teenager hears jokes about his religion in class, feels angry and ashamed, and a friend and teacher protect him by naming the stereotype as false.

passage:
Mehak, thanks for having me on. You asked what it's like being Christian in my town. Mostly fine. But I'll tell you about Class 10.
A rumour went round that Christians "pay people to convert." One boy asked, loudly, "So how much did your family get?" People laughed. I laughed too, which I hate now. Then I went home and didn't eat.
The next day, my friend Ruksana stood up in the canteen and said, "Devika's family has been Christian for five generations. She's my friend, and that rumour is rubbish." Our teacher, Mrs. Pillai, heard it and took the whole class through what stereotypes do. She said clearly the rumour was false.
I stopped laughing along after that. That's what I'd tell teenagers now: find the one friend and the one adult. It was the two of them that protected me. I'm Devika, by the way, if anyone's listening.

qa.q: How long has Devika's family been Christian?
qa.a: Devika's family has been Christian for five generations.

qa.q: Why did Devika laugh along and then not eat?
qa.a: Devika laughed to hide shame and hurt, and then felt so upset at home that she didn't eat.

qa.q: What made the difference for Devika?
qa.a: Ruksana spoke up publicly and Mrs. Pillai named the rumour as a false stereotype in front of the class, giving real protection.

qa.q: How might Ruksana have felt standing up in the canteen?
qa.a: Ruksana may have felt nervous but determined, angry at the rumour and protective of Devika.

grounding: A teenager hears a false rumour about her faith, feels ashamed and silenced, and is protected by a friend and a teacher who name it as false.

passage:
Monday. At lunch, a classmate saw Jatin's Jain tiffin with no onion or garlic and said, "Jains eat grass, right? And never spend a rupee." Everyone laughed. Jatin, fifteen, smiled stiffly and shut his tiffin.
Wednesday. The joke had spread. Someone left a handful of grass on his desk. Jatin skipped lunch and told nobody. His friend Chaitanya noticed him sitting alone in the library.
"Is it the grass thing?" Chaitanya asked. Jatin shrugged, eyes stinging. "It's just a joke."
"It's not funny if it's every day," Chaitanya said.
Thursday. Chaitanya went with Jatin to the class teacher. She listened, then spoke to the class that afternoon: "Mocking someone's faith, their food, or saying a whole community is stingy is a stereotype. It's untrue and it hurts." The grass stopped appearing.

qa.q: What was left on Jatin's desk?
qa.a: Someone left a handful of grass on his desk.

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling when he sat alone in the library?
qa.a: Jatin felt hurt and ashamed, his eyes stinging, though he tried to call it just a joke.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya help, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Chaitanya noticed Jatin alone, said daily jokes aren't funny, and went with him to the teacher, who named the stereotype as false in front of the class.

qa.q: How might the classmates see the joke after the teacher spoke?
qa.a: They may realise that what felt like harmless fun was hurting Jatin and was based on an untrue stereotype.

grounding: Over several days, a teenager hears mocking stereotypes about his faith, feels ashamed and silenced, and a friend and teacher protect him.

passage: Pranav, you asked if anyone ever teased me for being Hindu. Sit. I was fifteen, the only brown boy in my class in Leicester. One morning Gary held his nose when I opened my lunch and said my lot prayed to monkeys. The whole row laughed. I went hot, then silent. I wanted to disappear into my collar. Then Colin, a quiet boy who kept pigeons, said, "That's rubbish, Gary. You don't know a thing about it." At lunch Colin told Mr. Hughes, our teacher. That afternoon Mr. Hughes stopped the lesson and said plainly that what Gary had said was false and unkind, and asked if I'd like to tell the class about Diwali. I said no that day. The next year I said yes. Your Karthik Thatha still remembers Colin's pigeons, beta.

qa.q: Where was Karthik the only brown boy in his class?
qa.a: He was the only brown boy in his class in Leicester.

qa.q: What did young Karthik feel when the whole row laughed?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and silenced; he went hot, then quiet, and wanted to disappear into his collar.

qa.q: At the turning point in the story, why did Colin's choice matter?
qa.a: Colin spoke up in the moment and then told the teacher the same day, so Karthik was not alone and an adult could name the stereotype as false.

qa.q: How might Colin have seen what Gary did?
qa.a: Colin clearly saw it as ignorant and unfair, and though quiet, felt strongly enough to call it rubbish in front of everyone.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager mocked about his religion by classmates, and how a friend who spoke up and a teacher who named the stereotype as false protected him.
